archetype.name: Playoff Team (out-chancing, goalie-backed)
archetype.definition: A Boston side that wins the 5-on-5 chance battle and gets above-average goaltending from both netminders, but whose results are currently inflated by shooting and save percentages that sit near the top of the league.

report.headline: Better process than last year's 100-point team, but the percentages will cool
report.take:
Boston is 13-6-1 and fifth on the site, with the league's fourth-best Goal Diff / GP (+1.00), seventh-best offense and fourth-best defense. On the surface it looks like a carryover of last season's 100-point team. The engine is different, though. Last year's Bruins posted an xGF % of .473 and won on a PDO of 102.3 and 30.6 goals saved above expected, a goalie-driven team that was outplayed at 5-on-5. This year's xGF % is .538, fifth in the league. That is the most important number on the sheet: Boston is now creating the better chances, not just surviving them.

The percentages are flattering that improvement. Its 5-on-5 PDO is 104.2 and its all-situations PDO of 104.1 ranks second. The skaters are shooting 13.0% against a league mark of 11.4%, and the goalies are stopping .911 against .892. Shot volume is ordinary: 27.4 shots a game for, exactly league average, and 28.1 against, 22nd. Shot-attempt share is a flat 50%. So the goal margin is real in direction but too big in size. The depth scoring shows the same pattern. Casey Mittelstadt has 7 goals on 29 shots and James Hagens 6 on 34, rates few middle-six forwards hold.

What the record does not hide is luck in close games. Pts vs Goal Diff is -1.5, 25th in the league, so Boston has banked slightly fewer points than its goals imply. The 13-6-1 is not propped up by overtime coin flips. The two weak spots are special teams and the recent defensive form. The power play converts 18.5%, 25th and well under the league's 22.2%, which is odd for a group with David Pastrnak's 26 points leading it. Over the last five games Boston allowed 3.2 a game, 0.6 worse than its season rate, capped by 5-2 and 6-2 home losses to Montreal and Minnesota.

The outlook is a good, not dominant, team. As the shooting and save percentages drift toward normal, expect a goal margin closer to modest than elite. The 5-on-5 chance share and two goalies who both rank in the top 13 at their position give it a floor well inside the playoff picture in a crowded Atlantic, where four teams sit within a couple of points.

strengths.title: Now it out-chances opponents
strengths.body: Boston's 5-on-5 expected-goal share is .538, fifth in the league and a sharp turn from .473 last season. The chance quality is spread across the lineup: Elias Lindholm (.584), Mittelstadt (.587) and Charlie McAvoy (.628) all post strong on-ice shares. This is the most sustainable part of the profile, though it comes with only even shot-attempt share, so it rests on shot quality more than possession.

strengths.title: Two goalies, both above expected
strengths.body: The tandem has saved 10.9 goals above expected, fourth in the league, and the work is split. Jeremy Swayman is at +5.6 over 15 starts, and Michael DiPietro is at +5.1 with a .925 save % in five. Last year's +30.6 shows this group can sustain above-average work. Even so, DiPietro's rate in a small sample is the likeliest number on the roster to come down.

strengths.title: Defensemen and centers held quiet
strengths.body: Opposing defensemen produce well under their norms against Boston (second-best in the league), and centers rank fifth. The blueline's gaps are mostly closed, even with a B- grade. Wingers are where points leak: they take a larger share of the points against Boston than the league norm.

concerns.title: Percentages running well above normal
concerns.body: An all-situations PDO of 104.1, second in the league, comes from 13.0% shooting and .911 goaltending, both far above league averages. Neither shot volume nor shot suppression backs a margin this wide. Expect the goal differential to shrink even if the chance share holds.

concerns.title: Power play lagging the talent
concerns.body: An 18.5% power play ranks 25th, even with Pastrnak (9 PP points), Pavel Zacha and Morgan Geekie carrying it. Last year's unit hit 23.4%, so this looks more like slump than structure. Still, it is costing Boston goals in tight games.

concerns.title: Recent leaks on defense
concerns.body: Boston allowed 3.2 a game over the last five, 0.6 worse than its season rate, and dropped back-to-back home games by a combined lopsided margin. McAvoy has played 14 of 20 games but logs a team-high 24.28 minutes when in. How the pairs hold without him matters, because Mason Lohrei and Frederic Brunet sit below 50% in expected goals.

trend.note: A 9-5 October scoring 3.71 a game cooled to 3-2 in November with goals against rising to 3.2 a game. The last ten (6-4) still carry a positive differential, so this is a leveling off rather than a slide.

weekAhead.headline: Three soft defenses, two leaky penalty kills: a chance to reset
weekAhead.body:
The week opens at home against Los Angeles, 30th on the site, with F-graded goaltending (-8.9 GSAx) and a 67.2% penalty kill that ranks 29th. Then comes a road back-to-back in Detroit. The Red Wings score little (27th in offense) and allow only 24.4 shots a game, fourth-fewest, but their kill is 26th. Boston closes at home against Washington, a 10-8 team with a top-10 offense, a 28th-ranked defense and D-graded goaltending stopping .882.

All three opponents rank in the bottom third on the penalty kill or in goaltending, which suits a Boston attack that has been finishing well. The Capitals game is the real test: they out-chance teams too (.537 xGF %) and score enough to punish another loose night like the Montreal and Minnesota losses. Two wins are the baseline expectation, and three is realistic.

keyMatchups.title: Struggling power play meets bad kills
keyMatchups.body: Boston's 25th-ranked power play draws Los Angeles (29th on the PK) and Detroit (26th). If the unit cannot cash in here, the slump starts to look structural rather than variance.

keyMatchups.title: Pastrnak against Washington's wingers
keyMatchups.body: Washington gives wingers 4.56 points a game, 28th in the league. It also hands wingers far more of its points against than the league norm. That sets up well for Pastrnak and JJ Peterka on the right side.

keyMatchups.title: Back-to-back in Detroit
keyMatchups.body: The Detroit game comes the night after Los Angeles, which likely means a DiPietro start for one of them. Detroit limits shots well, so a grinding, low-event game is the likely shape. Boston's finishing edge matters more there than volume.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the goals-against trend from the last five games reverses against three weaker offenses, or whether the defensive loosening is real.

restOfSeason.body: The 82-game pace of 111 points rests on a top-two PDO, and that will come down. The xGF % of .538 is a genuine upgrade on last year. Two goalies performing above expected and a deep group of centers (seven listed, all contributing) make a winning record over the remaining 62 games very likely. Because Pts vs Goal Diff is negative, there is no close-game luck to give back; the regression will come through goals, not through overtime results. A rebound on the power play toward last year's level would offset much of the shooting-percentage drop. Expect something around 100 points and a playoff spot in a tight Atlantic.
swingFactors: How far shooting % and save % fall toward league average
Power play recovering toward last year's 23.4%
McAvoy's availability and minutes on a B- blueline

confidence.note: Twenty games; chance share supports the record but PDO inflates the margin.
